title: Microfluidic Tools for Probing Fungal-Microbial Interactions at the Cellular Level
protocol: Prepare a 100 mm silicon wafer by baking in an oven at 200 °C for 2 hours.
Spin-coat the silicon wafer with SU-8 2010 photoresist to achieve a target thickness of 10 µm, starting at 500 rpm for 10 seconds and accelerating to 3,000 rpm for 45 seconds.
Bake the coated silicon wafer at 95 °C for 2.5 minutes (soft bake).
Expose the photoresist to ultraviolet light using a film photolithography mask with an energy dose of 140 mJ/cm² at 365 nm wavelength.
Bake the coated silicon wafer at 95 °C for 3.5 minutes (post exposure bake).
Immerse and agitate the silicon wafer in developer solution for 3 minutes to reveal microfabricated structures by removing unexposed photoresist.
Rinse with fresh developer solution for 10 s.
Rinse with isopropyl alcohol for 10 s.
Air dry using filtered compressed air.
Measure the height of the SU-8 structures, for example, using a profilometer.
Silanize each master mold with 50 µL of chlorotrimethylsilane by applying a vacuum pressure of 50 mbar for 2 h.
Prepare approximately 40 g of PDMS by thoroughly mixing the base and curing agent in a 10:1 ratio using a spatula in a clean plastic cup.
Degas the mixture to remove all air bubbles by placing the plastic cup into a vacuum chamber (vacuum pressure = 50 mbar) for 1 h.
Secure the master mold into a plastic mount using clear tape.
Clean the master mold using compressed filtered air to remove any dust particles.
Pour the PDMS mixture onto the center of the master mold on a level surface.
Allow the PDMS mixture to settle.
Cover the master mold loosely with a plastic lid.
Transfer the master mold to an oven and cure overnight at 70 °C.
Remove the master mold from the oven and allow it to cool.
Peel the cured PDMS away from the master mold, taking care not to damage either the master mold or the PDMS.
Place clear tape over the microchannels embossed into the PDMS.
Cut the PDMS into slabs using a mounted guillotine or razor blade.
When cutting the lateral opening of the BFI PDMS slab, ensure that the microchannels are fully open.
For the FFI PDMS slab, trim each corner to fit it into the glass-bottomed Petri dish.
Punch inlet and outlet holes according to the device design.
Use a precision cutter to punch 3.18 mm inlet holes for BFI devices.
Use a precision cutter to punch 4.75 mm inlet holes for FFI devices.
Submerge PDMS slabs in 0.5 M NaOH and sonicate for 5 min.
Rinse PDMS slabs with sterile ddH2O.
Transfer PDMS slabs into 70% ethanol solution and sonicate for 5 min.
Rinse PDMS slabs with sterile ddH2O.
Immerse PDMS slabs in sterile ddH2O and sonicate for 5 min.
Remove PDMS slabs from the sterile ddH2O.
Dry PDMS slabs using filtered compressed air.
Place PDMS slabs into a sterile square Petri dish.
Place the Petri dish containing PDMS slabs into an oven at 70 °C for 1 h.
Remove PDMS slabs from the oven and allow to cool in a dust-free environment.
Clear any dust from the surface of PDMS slabs using tape and/or filtered compressed air.
Activate the surfaces of PDMS slabs and glass-bottomed Petri dishes using a plasma cleaner at vacuum pressure 0.75 mbar, power 50%, coating time 1 min.
Remove the PDMS slabs and glass-bottomed Petri dishes from the plasma cleaner.
Gently place the activated surfaces into conformal contact with the 35 mm and 50 mm diameter glass-bottomed Petri dishes for BFI and FFI PDMS slabs, respectively.
Take care not to apply too much pressure when bonding to avoid collapse of the microchannels.
Check for successful bonding by trying to pull the PDMS slab off the glass-bottomed Petri dish with tweezers.
Visualize the devices by eye or using microscopy to ensure no collapse of the inoculation inlets or microchannels.
For saturated conditions, include step 2.2.7 of the protocol.
If water-unsaturated conditions are required, proceed to step 2.2.8.
Fill the BFI device with 100 µL of the desired solution for bacterial inlet and lateral opening immediately after bonding.
Fill the FFI device by pipetting 30 µL of media into each inlet (60 µL total) immediately after bonding.
If air bubbles are present, they will dissipate around 10 min after filling due to PDMS porosity.
Add sterile ddH2O (~100-200 µL) in the Petri dish to maintain humidity.
Prepare desired culture medium supplemented with agar.
Autoclave the medium at 121 °C for 15 min.
Allow the medium to cool to 50 °C and pour into 9 cm diameter Petri dishes, maintaining sterile conditions.
Remove a 4 mm diameter plug of agar containing mycelium from a fridge stock colony of the desired fungal strain.
Place the side of the plug with mycelium in contact with the agar surface in the center of the uninoculated Petri dish.
Replace the lid on top of the Petri dish and seal before incubating at the appropriate temperature for the desired strain for the required amount of time.
Streak out the desired bacterial isolate onto an agar plate to achieve single bacterial colonies.
Seal the plate with film.
Incubate at a temperature and duration specific to the isolate until individual colonies are observed.
Prepare 1 L of LB medium by adding 10 g of tryptone, 10 g of NaCl, and 5 g of yeast extract per liter of ddH2O.
Autoclave the medium at 121 °C for 15 min.
Allow the medium to cool to room temperature.
Add the cooled medium to a sterile culture flask inside a sterile environment.
Touch a single bacterial colony from the agar plate using a sterile inoculation loop.
Transfer the inoculated loop into the sterile culture medium by briefly touching the liquid with the loop.
Seal the flask using a sterile lid or foil.
Place the flask in a shaking incubator overnight using settings appropriate for B. subtilis, such as 37 °C at 200 rpm for liquid cultures.
Use a sterilized cork borer (ø = 4 mm) to remove an agar plug from the colony on the periphery of a 3-day-old culture.
Ensure that the growing hyphal front remains intact.
Introduce the plug into the fungal inlet, mycelium side down, with the growth direction oriented toward the microchannel openings.
Repeat steps for the second fungal species if using the FFI device.
If using the BFI device, omit this step and continue to step 4.1.4.
Seal the Petri dish with transparent film.
Incubate at 25-28 °C in the dark until imaging commences.
Determine the pre-imaging incubation time based on the intended biological event and growth rate of included species within the device.
Dilute bacteria from an overnight culture in a 1:25 ratio using the same culture medium as detailed previously.
Culture for 3 h at 37 °C.
Wash the bacteria by pelleting culture using a centrifuge at 2000 x g for 10 min.
Discard the supernatant and resuspend the cells in desired volume of 0.9% w/v sodium chloride solution.
Centrifuge again to obtain a pellet.
Discard the supernatant and resuspend the cells in liquid medium (e.g., C. cinerea minimal medium) to an OD600 of 1.
Optimize the OD600 value for the bacterial strain in question.
Remove the BFI device from the incubator and open it in a sterile environment.
Pipette 10 µL of suspension into the bacterial inlet.
Seal the Petri dish with a transparent film.
Incubate at 25 °C in the dark until imaging commences.
Store the device upright.
Turn on the microscope computer, microscope main body (if applicable), camera, temperature-controlled incubator, and light source(s).
Ensure that the microscope has been set up correctly, e.g., Köhler illumination has been correctly applied for even illumination of the sample.
Initiate the imaging software package.
Mount the microfluidic device into the stage insert.
Secure the device with tape to prevent dislodging during movement.
Acquire images of the inoculated devices using phase contrast microscopy.
Use autofocus software and either 10x or 20x magnification lenses for imaging.
Excite fluorescent reporter proteins using a high-power LED light engine with specific wavelengths.
Export acquired images into TIFF format for subsequent analysis.
Download Fiji software.
Install and launch Fiji.
Import an image sequence from a time-lapse experiment.
Select File > Import > Image Sequence.
Locate the folder containing the data.
Open the folder to import the images.
In the Sequence Options window, select Preferences.
Click OK in the Sequence Options window.
Select the Straight Line icon from the main toolbar.
Position the beginning of the straight line at the tip of the growing hypha by clicking and dragging.
Drag the cursor to another point within the frame to set the end of the line.
Move to the next frame in the image sequence by pressing Ctrl and > simultaneously.
Position the end of the straight line at the new position of the growing hyphal tip by selecting and dragging the square box.
Press and hold Ctrl and M to measure the length of the line in pixels.
A Results window will appear displaying the measured data.
Define the data displayed in the Results window as needed.
Click on the Results window.
Select Results > Set Measurements from the menu.
Press and hold Ctrl and then M to measure the length of the line in pixels.
Select all of the data in the Results window.
Copy and paste the data into another software programme, e.g., a spreadsheet.
Plot the hyphal growth (in pixels or micrometres) as a function of time.
Calculate the average growth rates.
Perform at least three biological replicates per experiment.
Download Fiji.
Install and launch Fiji.
Import image sequence from a time-lapse experiment by selecting File > Import > Image Sequence.
Locate the folder where the data is stored and select Open.
Select Preferences in the Sequence Options window and then OK.
Specify a region of interest (ROI) to measure the absolute fluorescence intensity of a hypha using the rectangular tool located in the main toolbar.
Define the size of the square exactly as follows: Edit > Selection > Specify.
Save the ROI for future reference in the ROI Manager by selecting Edit > Selection > Add to Manager.
Measure the absolute fluorescence intensity within the defined ROI for each image in the entire image sequence or stack.
Open the Image > Stacks > Measure Stack menu option.
Copy all data from the Results window once processing is complete.
Paste the copied data into a spreadsheet program.
Plot the absolute fluorescence intensities of the specified ROI as a function of time.
Repeat steps to collect absolute fluorescence intensity measurements for each ROI.

Calculate relative fluorescence intensities in arbitrary units by dividing the absolute fluorescence intensity of the ROI [hypha of interest] by the absolute fluorescence intensity of the ROI [control channel].
Perform at least three biological replicates per experiment.
Plot the relative fluorescence intensities as a function of time.
